The role of an insurance company is to cover loss. Covering loss generally means monetary payment. Therefore an insurance company must collect fees called premiums from the insured. By investing stored capital, an insurance company can operate while paying out more in covered loss than it brings in through premiums. But only to a limit. Therefore, the insurance company needs to set premium rates appropriate to expected loss.

Once a an insurance company has *experience* in the form of a history of claims and payments, the most sensible way to determine expected loss is through *statistical modeling*. It is possible to do this through *statistical analysis* such as numerically calculating statistical quantities. Nevertheless, we will discuss reasons why it is more advantageous to calculate these quantities using models rather than direct computation.

At any point in time, an insurer's accountants can tally up the losses paid out to the premiums collected and determine if the company is making a profit. Whatever the overall outcome of that calculation is, the individual contribution to that number from different products and coverages remains important. Therefore, pricing modelers want to assess the profitability of individual policies. The simplest approach is to determine a ratio called AvT or Actual versus Technical. Actual refers to the actual premium collected by the insurance company. Technical refers to an idealized premium that *should* be (or *should have been*) charged to cover the losses that policy incurred. To determine how things went in the past, this can be calculated on historical claims. To anticipate how things will go in the future, this must be calculated on expected losses.

$x_{i\nu}$ is observation i of variable $\nu$. $x_{\cdot \nu}$ is a column vector of observations of variable $\nu$. $x_{i \cdot}$ is a row vector of observation i of all variables. In computer science, if we have a vector `v = [...]` we allow "indexing" the vector with another vector that represents the coordinates we want to address. So if `v = [2, 9, 3, 1, 100, 2]` and `x = [3,1]`, then `v[x]` returns `[3,2]`. Here I'm assuming the 1-based indexing of R and MatLab rather than the 0–based indexing of Python and C. We will employ a similar system here. Let $S$ be a set of indices. Then $x_{i[S]}$ is the coordinates of observation $i$ selected by the indices in $S$. Furthermore, $x_{i[\S]}$ is exactly the coordinates NOT in the set $S$. For simplicity, we will use uppercase letters for index sets and drop the square brackets. Thus, $x_{i\cdot} \equiv (x_{iS},x{i\S})$. But because S can be any indices, that noation looks funny becasuse we aer not repseting the actual ordering of the indices. We are accustomed to depicting vectors as ordered sets of coordinates. If I write $x = (1, 9, 11, 100, 2, 27)$ then we understand that $x_1 = 1, x_2 = 9, x_3 = 11$ and so on. In computer programming, when you define a function that takes three arguments `f(x1,x2,x3)`, then when you call it `f(1,9,11)`, `x1,x2,x3` are assigned the values `(1,9,11)` respectively.

Many computer languages also allow keyword arguments. In this case, we would be free to call the function like `f(x3=11, x1=1, x2=9)` and receive the same output. Some computer languages also allow destructuring assignments that work like this: `(x3,x1,x2) = (11,1,9)`. Now, suppose `x1,x2,x3` are references and we define `x = [x1,x2,x3]` In this case, the following assignments are equivalent:
